title: Efficient Stochastic Optimisation via Sequential Monte Carlo
topic: Probabilistic Methods->Monte Carlo and Sampling Methods
claim: Our SMC-based optimisers converge faster and more stably in wall-clock time than inner-loop sampling baselines across optimiser and objective settings.
layout: 2x2 grid of line plots, (a)/(b) rows, shared legends above each row
description: Four line plots in two rows, labeled (a) and (b). Each row has a shared legend above it with six methods: ImpDiff, SOUL and four SOSMC variants (HMC, ULA, MALA, RWM). The legend is paired with SGD in row (a) and Adam in row (b). The left plot of each row shows mean reward against time in seconds. The right plot shows an NLL proxy against time. Shaded bands show variability across runs. In (a), the dashed SOSMC curves rise quickly and plateau near 0.64 reward, while SOUL is very noisy and ImpDiff is slow. ImpDiff's NLL dips sharply to about -5.6 before recovering. In (b), the solid SOSMC-HMC and SOSMC-RWM curves stabilise quickly. SOSMC-ULA is noisy and lower, and ImpDiff and SOUL stay near zero reward. Teal, orange, magenta, purple, black and bright green lines are the main colors.
caption: Wall-clock convergence of mean reward (left) and NLL (right), across $10$ runs, for \gls*{ImpDiff}, \gls*{SOUL}, and \gls*{SOSMC} variants under different $\mathrm{OPT}$ for (a) $V_{\mathrm{dual}}$ & $R_{\mathrm{smooth}}$; (b) $V_{\mathrm{tight}}$ & $R_{\mathrm{tight}}$.
abstract: The problem of optimising functions with intractable gradients frequently arises in machine learning and statistics, ranging from maximum marginal likelihood estimation procedures to fine-tuning of generative models. Stochastic approximation methods for this class of problems typically require inner sampling loops to obtain (biased) stochastic gradient estimates, which rapidly becomes computationally expensive. In this work, we develop sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) samplers for optimisation of functions with intractable gradients. Our approach replaces expensive inner sampling methods with efficient SMC approximations, which can result in significant computational gains. We establish convergence results for the basic recursions defined by our methodology which SMC samplers approximate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the reward-tuning of energy-based models within various settings.
